title: Why adding threads didn't speed up your Python
description:
STYLE SAMPLE -- stick-figure animation test. You added threading and got zero speedup. The Global Interpreter Lock is why, and multiprocessing is the fix.

Source lesson:
- https://sigilipelli.github.io/python-mastery-path/level-3/04-concurrency-threading-multiprocessing/

#Shorts

beats.narration: You added threading to make your Python code faster, and it ran exactly as slowly as before. Here's why that happens.
Python has one lock, called the GIL. Only the thread holding it can run Python code. The others just wait their turn.
So four threads on a pure counting loop don't split that work four ways. They politely take turns holding the very same lock.

display.code:
def cpu_bound(n):
    count = 0
    for _ in range(n):
        count += 1
    return count

threads = [threading.Thread(target=cpu_bound, args=(20_000_000,))
           for _ in range(4)]

beats.narration: Four threads, and barely faster than doing it one at a time.

display.output: threaded: 3.71s   # not much faster than sequential

beats.narration: The fix is multiprocessing. Separate processes, each with its own interpreter and its own lock, genuinely running across your cores.
Same function, a process pool instead of threads, and now it actually scales with your core count.

display.code:
with multiprocessing.Pool(processes=4) as pool:
    results = pool.map(cpu_bound, [20_000_000] * 4)

beats.narration: So: threading for waiting on input and output, multiprocessing for real CPU work. Full lesson is linked below.
